extracted.intended_audience: literate early-18th-century British readers interested in literature, manners, theatre, and fashion
extracted.subtask_description: Literary criticism outlining technical criteria for judging epic poetry (using Paradise Lost, the Iliad, and the Aeneid as examples); the page also contains ancillary guidance on fashion (hood colours), moral judgment, acting, and tavern provisioning. Primary focus: rules for what makes an epic poem successful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action (One Action)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fable (action) of an epic poem should be but One Action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Homer and Virgil: open in medias res to preserve unity. Example: Homer begins with the princes' discord; Virgil opens with Aeneas near Italy because the poem celebrates his settlement. Milton likewise opens with the Infernal Council because the Fall of Man is the single action to be celebrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entire Action (Beginning, Middle, End)
rubrics_metrics.description: An epic's Action must be entire — complete in all its parts, consisting of a beginning, a middle, and an end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nothing should go before it, be intermixed with it, or follow after it that is not related to it; no single step of the progress from origin to consummation should be omitted. Examples: Achilles' anger and Aeneas's settlement show full progress; Milton's action is contrived in Hell, executed on Earth, and punished by Heaven.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greatness of Action (Magnitude and Consequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The action treated should be great in nature (consequence) — affecting persons, nations, or the whole species — and in duration (length) appropriate to an epic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Achilles' anger embroils Greek kings; Aeneas's settlement produces the Roman empire; Milton's subject concerns the fate of the whole human species. Greatness also involves suitable duration — not so short the memory loses detail, nor so long it cannot be contained by memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate Length / Due Duration
rubrics_metrics.description: An epic must have a due length: neither too short (so the mind cannot form distinct ideas of parts) nor too long (so memory cannot contain the whole).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle's simile: an animal too small or too large fails the eye; similarly action must be of a size fit for memory. Homer and Virgil extend short actions with episodes and machinery; Milton supplies a variety of incidents to occupy memory without overcharging it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnificence of Parts (Greatness in Principal Members)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not only the whole but the principal members and every part of an epic should be great and magnificent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parts (episodes, similes, scenes) should exhibit grandeur appropriate to the epic style. Addison notes Paradise Lost has an unquestionable magnificence in every part exceeding pagan systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Episodes (Must Arise Naturally and Relate to Principal Action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodes are allowable when they naturally arise from the subject and bear affinity with the principal action; they should not break the unity of the fable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homer and Virgil use episodes (e.g., Troy narratives, voyages) to diversify and extend the action without destroying unity; Milton casts earlier events into later books as episodes that run parallel to and illuminate the main action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect Source Material When Inventing Incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: When an epic is based on sacred or limited traditions, the poet must be cautious in adding invented incidents to avoid offending religion or truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton had few traditional materials and so needed extreme care in his inventions; despite restraints, he filled his poem with surprising incidents closely analogous to scripture and acceptable to delicate readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hood Colour Should Complement Complexion (Fashion Advice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select head-dress (hood) colours to suit a lady's complexion so the hood enhances rather than clashes with the face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two sets of rules are cited: Ovid recommends red-striped silk for pale complexions, white for brown, and dark for the fair; Will Honeycomb (a contemporary arbiter) suggests palest features look best in white sarsenet, overflushed faces in deep scarlet, and darkest complexions are alleviated by black. The general aim: choose hood colour to lose or soften the colour of the face by contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Head-dress Colours as Signals (Social/Political Signalling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hood colours may function as signals of party, mood, or intention among women — effectively communicating social or political allegiance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: Whig and Tory ladies reportedly display different colours; colours can be used as gallant signals (e.g., a woman in white signals tranquility; flame colour signifies resolution). Anecdotes: a lady intending to appear in a rainbow hood or Cornelia habitually in black when her husband is away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperate Moral Judgment — Compassion over Condemnation
rubrics_metrics.description: No natural vice ought to place a person wholly beneath the compassion of the virtuous; condemn the act but pity the person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steele argues modest women should hate breaches of chastity for themselves but pity others; denounces the 'outragiously virtuous' who react without mercy. He emphasizes understanding circumstances (poverty, coercion) and not excluding compassionate treatment for those who fall into vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting Skill Valued by Public Approbation and Mimicry
rubrics_metrics.description: An actor's pride and measure of success is the approbation of critics and spectators; skill in mimicry is prized and socially rewarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richard Estcourt's mimicry and ability to assume the Spectator's air is described as diverting; actors and players seek approbation (the Spectator's favour) and social recognition — a practical criterion of theatrical merit in the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tavern Provisioning and Service Standards (Practical Commerce Advice)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reputable tavern should stock 'neat natural wines' fresh and in perfection, source reliably from known merchants, sell wholesale and retail, and deliver drinks in natural purity with faithful service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estcourt's Bumper Tavern advertises wines bought from reputable merchants (Brooke and Hellier), sold wholesale and retail with fidelity by an old servant; promises fresh supplies and hopes friends/customers will reward good service. This operates as a standard for a respectable tavern-business.
